bigPicture.subtitle: Through Suffering to Glory, Held by a Living Hope
bigPicture.thesis: If we had to summarize the Book of 1 Peter in one overarching thought, it is this: because God has given you new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus, you can live as a holy exile in a hostile world — doing good, blessing those who curse you, following the steps of the suffering Christ, and entrusting your soul to a faithful Creator — knowing that after a little while of suffering comes eternal glory.
paragraphs: First Peter was written to Christians who had lost their place in society. They had turned from the idols and the parties of their towns, and their neighbours now called them strange, slandered them and sometimes made them suffer. Peter did not tell them to fight back, withdraw or blend in. He told them who they were — chosen, born again, a royal priesthood, God's own people — and how to live: holy, humble, good and hopeful, following the steps of a Saviour who suffered first.

The letter is built on one pattern, which Peter states in the first chapter: “the sufferings of Christ, and the glories that would follow them” (1 Peter 1:11). What was true of Christ becomes true of His people. They suffer “for a little while” (1 Peter 1:6), and they are called “to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus” (1 Peter 5:10). Every chapter moves along that line: from the trial that proves faith like gold to the crown of glory that never fades.

The writer's own story is written between the lines. Peter had once rebuked Jesus for speaking of the cross, slept in Gethsemane, drawn a sword, denied his Lord with curses and wept bitterly. The risen Christ restored him with three questions and three commands to feed His sheep. In this letter the restored shepherd feeds the flock. He writes as “a witness of the sufferings of Christ” (1 Peter 5:1), and as a man who knew what it was for a dead hope to come alive.

Peter's name means ‘rock’, yet he never claims to be the foundation. He gives that place to Christ, “a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious” (1 Peter 2:4), and makes every believer a living stone in the same house. The letter's last word is the promise he himself had experienced: the God of all grace will “perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you” (1 Peter 5:10) — the God who mends broken fishermen mends broken nets.

map.intro: First Peter is the twenty-first book of the New Testament, the second of the letters written to the scattered church. It stands after James and before 2 Peter, and it is written to the same people James addressed — believers in ‘the Dispersion’.

sections.title: James Tested Faith; Peter Anchored Hope
sections.body: James and 1 Peter share many themes: joy in trials, faith proved like gold, humility before God, resisting the devil, and good works. Both quote Proverbs 3:34. But their emphasis differs. James asks, ‘Is your faith real? Show it by works.’ Peter asks, ‘How do you keep going when your faith costs you everything?’ and answers with hope: a living hope, an unfading inheritance and a coming glory. Read together, they give the church both a test and a hope.

sections.title: Israel's Titles for the Whole Church
sections.body: Peter applies to a largely Gentile church the titles God gave Israel at Sinai: “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). He quotes Hosea's reversal — “who in time past were no people, but now are God’s people” (1 Peter 2:10) — and calls them exiles of the Dispersion. The story of Israel, with its exodus, wilderness wandering and exile, has become the story of every believer: redeemed by the blood of a lamb, on pilgrimage, awaiting the true homeland.

sections.title: Hard Passages Read Honestly
sections.body: First Peter contains some of the most debated verses in the New Testament. This study has given the strongest reading and named the alternatives. The ‘spirits in prison’ (3:19) are most likely the rebellious spirits of Noah's day, to whom the risen Christ proclaimed His victory; others hold different views, but Scripture nowhere offers a second chance after death. Baptism ‘saves’ (3:21) not as a washing but as a good conscience's pledge to God through Christ's resurrection. The gospel preached ‘to the dead’ (4:6) most likely means to believers who heard it in life and have since died. And ‘Babylon’ (5:13) is almost certainly a code name for Rome.

sections.title: Word Families in 1 Peter
sections.body: First Peter added three new word families to this study: birth (ἀναγεννάω ‘born again’, ἀρτιγέννητος ‘newborn’, with γεννάω, ἀποκυέω and τίκτω), redeem (λυτρόω, λύτρον, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἀγοράζω, ἐξαγοράζω) and suffer (πάσχω, πάθημα, συμπάσχω, κακοπαθέω) — Peter's own vocabulary of suffering. Its key contrasts include τηρέω and φρουρέω (the inheritance kept, the heirs guarded, 1:4–5), καιρός and χρόνος (1:5, 1:17), φιλαδελφία and ἀγάπη (1:22), λόγος and ῥῆμα (1:23, 25), ἀποκαλύπτω and φανερόω (1:20; 5:1, 4), ὑπογραμμός and τύπος (2:21; 5:3) and ἰσχύς and κράτος (4:11).

roadAhead.intro: The Road Ahead: 1 Peter ended with suffering for a little while, eternal glory, and a God who establishes His people. The next two books are 2 Peter, Peter's last letter, written as he faced death, warning against false teachers and calling believers to grow while they wait for the day of the Lord; and 1 John, a letter about fellowship with God, walking in the light, love for one another and assurance of eternal life.

books.connection: Peter writes again: “This is now, beloved, the second letter that I have written to you; and in both of them I stir up your sincere mind by reminding you” (2 Peter 3:1). He knows his death is near: “knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me” (2 Peter 1:14). The first letter dealt with pressure from outside — persecution; the second deals with danger from inside — false teachers. He begins with God's provision: “seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness” (2 Peter 1:3), and calls believers to add virtue to faith in a ladder of growth. He writes again as an eyewitness: “we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1:16). And the hope of 1 Peter becomes the hope of a new creation: “But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). Watch for how Peter guards the truth while the church waits.

John, Peter's companion in the boat, at the tomb and before the council, writes as an eyewitness too: “That which was from the beginning, that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). Peter called believers born again; John explores what it means to be children of God: “See how great a love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God!” (1 John 3:1). Peter commanded fervent love; John says, “He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love” (1 John 4:8). And where Peter gave hope to the suffering, John gives assurance to the doubting: “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). Watch for the tests of true faith John gives — truth, obedience and love.

themesMastered.title: A Living Hope and an Unfading Inheritance
themesMastered.body: God “caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3), to an inheritance that cannot decay, be stained or fade, kept in heaven — while believers themselves are guarded by God's power through faith. Trials for a little while prove faith like gold in the fire, and result in praise and glory when Christ is revealed. Believers love Him without having seen Him, and rejoice with joy beyond words.

themesMastered.title: Holy Exiles, Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood
themesMastered.body: Because God is holy, His people are to be holy in all their conduct (1 Peter 1:15–16), knowing they were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ. Born again of imperishable seed, they crave the word like newborns, and are built as living stones into a spiritual house on Christ, the rejected but precious cornerstone. They are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), called to proclaim His excellence.

themesMastered.title: Good Conduct Before a Watching World
themesMastered.body: As foreigners, believers abstain from fleshly desires and live such good lives that slanderers see their good works and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). They respect authority, serve faithfully even under harsh masters, win unbelieving spouses without a word, honour their wives as co-heirs, bless those who insult them, and are always ready to give a gentle answer “concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15).

themesMastered.title: Following the Steps of the Suffering Christ
themesMastered.body: Christ suffered for us, leaving an example: no sin, no deceit, no curse in return, but trust in the righteous Judge (1 Peter 2:21–23). He bore our sins on the tree and by His wounds we are healed. He suffered once for sins to bring us to God, and now reigns with every power subject to Him. So believers arm themselves with His mind, are not surprised by the fiery trial, rejoice to share His sufferings, and “entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator” (1 Peter 4:19).

themesMastered.title: Humility, Vigilance and the God of All Grace
themesMastered.body: Elders shepherd God's flock as willing servants and examples. All believers clothe themselves with humility, for God opposes the proud. They humble themselves under God's mighty hand, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7), stay sober and watchful, and resist the prowling lion, firm in faith. And the God of all grace, after a little while, will perfect, establish, strengthen and settle them.

experientialLesson.intro: How do you walk out the Book of 1 Peter practically moving forward? Here is your experiential blueprint:

steps.title: Live From Your Identity, Not Your Circumstances
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9).
steps.practice: The Practice: Each morning for the next month, before checking your phone, read 1 Peter 1:3–5 and 2:9 aloud and say: ‘I am born again to a living hope. I am chosen, royal, holy and God's own. My inheritance is kept and I am guarded.’ When criticism, rejection or hardship comes during the day, return to those words before you respond.

steps.title: Answer Insult With Blessing and Good Works
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing; knowing that to this were you called, that you may inherit a blessing” (1 Peter 3:9).
steps.practice: The Practice: Identify one person who has mistreated or slandered you. For thirty days, pray a specific blessing over them each day, and look for one concrete good work you can do for them or in their sight. Prepare your two-minute answer about the hope within you (3:15), and ask God for an opportunity to share it with gentleness.

steps.title: Cast, Watch and Entrust
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7), and “entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator” (1 Peter 4:19).
steps.practice: The Practice: Every evening this month, write down your worries and throw them onto God one by one in prayer, then pray Jesus' words, ‘Father, into Your hands I commit my spirit.’ Meet weekly with at least one other believer for prayer, so that you are never alone when the lion prowls. When suffering comes, say aloud: ‘This is for a little while; His glory is eternal.’

finalDeclaration: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to Your great mercy You have caused me to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. I declare that my inheritance is incorruptible, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for me, and that I am guarded by Your power through faith. My trials are for a little while, and they are proving my faith more precious than gold. I love Jesus though I have not seen Him, and I rejoice with joy beyond words. I was redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb, so I will be holy in all my conduct, because You are holy. I am a living stone in Your spiritual house, a member of a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, Your own possession, and I will proclaim the excellence of the One who called me out of darkness into His marvellous light. I will live as a pilgrim, abstaining from desires that war against my soul and doing good before a watching world. When I am insulted, I will bless. I will follow the steps of Jesus, who did not sin, did not curse back and did not threaten, but entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge; He bore my sins on the tree, and by His wounds I am healed. I set Christ apart as Lord in my heart, and I will be ready to give an answer for the hope within me, with gentleness and respect. I will not be surprised by the fiery trial; I will rejoice to share Christ's sufferings, for the Spirit of glory rests on me. I clothe myself with humility, I humble myself under Your mighty hand, and I cast all my worries on You, because You care for me. I will stay sober and watchful and resist the devil, firm in faith. And I declare that after I have suffered a little while, You, the God of all grace, will perfect, establish, strengthen and settle me. To You be the glory and the power forever and ever. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”
